summary: The database layer is a thin async adapter (apps/core/src/db.ts) over mysql2 3.24.6. It uses one pool of 10 connections against a single MySQL 8.0.46 instance (schema stonehash_attest) that shares the 4-CPU, 15 GB box with everything else, and the config file in /etc/mysql is stock. The code treats MySQL as the production engine, even though the README still says SQLite. SQLite (node:sqlite) is used only by tests and as a fallback. On SQLite every statement and transaction runs one at a time through a single promise chain. Nothing like that exists on MySQL, where up to 10 statements run at once and only four operations, all in service.ts, use transactions. There is no row locking, compare-and-set or deadlock retry anywhere. The schema has 21 InnoDB utf8mb4_bin tables. They key rows on random v4 UUID strings and store timestamps as ISO VARCHAR(40), hashes as hex text, money as VARCHAR strings, and every JSON document as-is in MEDIUMTEXT. Foreign keys are enforced. Single-row lookups and keyset paging are well indexed, and no transaction stays open across a network call. High volume causes trouble in four places. (1) The batch worker reads the whole attestations table on every tick (the inscription poll). It also seals at most one batch of up to 1,024 leaves per tick, with 2N+1 separate database calls per batch, so sealing tops out near 341/s and slows as the table grows. (2) Every audited request writes an audit row before it replies, API reads included. The remit rail runs about 150 statements and about 60 separately committed writes per payment. (3) The console, billing and ledger endpoints count each organisation's entire history, use date filters that cannot use an index, search JSON payloads with JSON_EXTRACT, and run one subquery whose cost grows with the square of the number of exhausted webhooks. All of this shares the same 10 connections. (4) Nothing is purged or partitioned except free-tier records. Under the owner's rule that organisation records never expire, storage grows in a straight line with volume: attestations alone add about 95 GB a year at T1 and about 9.5 TB at T2, and a remit payment costs roughly 20 to 30 times more bytes than an attestation. T1 is reachable once the per-tick full scan is removed and the webhook outbox is fixed. T2 needs bulk batch writes, a transaction with a state check for each remit step, counter tables in place of whole-history counts, a larger pool, and a tuned or dedicated MySQL. T3 needs workers that are safe with several app instances, time partitioning with archiving, read replicas, and an org_id shard key.

components.name: Storage adapter
components.role: Single async Db interface (prepare().get/all/run, exec, tx) with two engines; schema bootstrap and column/index migrations at boot
components.tech: mysql2/promise 3.24.6 pool (execute = server-side prepared statements, per-connection LRU 16000); node:sqlite DatabaseSync
components.notes: MySQL: createPool({waitForConnections:true, connectionLimit:10, charset:'utf8mb4_bin'}), no queueLimit (unbounded), no acquire timeout, no isolation level set (InnoDB default REPEATABLE READ), tx() = getConnection+beginTransaction+commit/rollback, no retry. SQLite: one promise chain serialises every statement; tx holds the queue slot. Bootstrap: 21 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, 17 ADD COLUMN checks via information_schema, 12 secondary indexes via catalogue check, CLEAR_ORG_EXPIRY UPDATE on every boot.

components.name: MySQL instance
components.role: Sole production store (primary only, no replica)
components.notes: Config file sets only bind-address, key_buffer_size, max_binlog_size=100M, log_error, so stock defaults apply (128 MB buffer pool, flush_log_at_trx_commit=1, sync_binlog=1, binlog ROW/FULL, max_connections 151, max_prepared_stmt_count 16382). Live values not verified (SET PERSIST possible). Shares a 4-CPU/15 GB box with Node, bitcoind, anvil and the web apps; 572 GB disk free.

components.name: Attest tables
components.role: attestations (one row per record), batches, merkle_proofs (one per leaf), anchor_txs (one per batch)
components.tech: InnoDB; attestations PK id VARCHAR(64) random UUID, rowseq BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT UNIQUE, UNIQUE(org_id, leaf_bytes CHAR(64)), FK org/batch; 6 secondary indexes
components.notes: Indexes: attestations_open(batch_id,status), attestations_open_order(batch_id,created_at), attestations_expiry(expires_at), attestations_org_created(org_id,created_at); anchor_txs_pending(status); InnoDB auto-creates FK indexes merkle_proofs(batch_id), anchor_txs(batch_id). batches has no status index. No index leads on kind, status, source or reveal_txid.

components.name: Tenancy and auth tables
components.role: orgs, api_keys, accounts, sessions, issuer_keys, subscriptions
components.tech: orgs.slug UNIQUE; api_keys.key_hash UNIQUE VARCHAR(128); accounts.email UNIQUE; sessions PK token_hash + sessions_expiry; subscriptions UNIQUE(org_id,product)
components.notes: Every keyed request does 1 lookup by key_hash; every console request does 2 primary-key lookups (session, account). Nothing caches them.

components.name: Audit trail
components.role: audit_log: one row per audited request (API key or console session), written before the response
components.tech: PK id = randomUUID; index audit_log_org_at(org_id, at, id); keyset search
components.notes: Only console screen GETs and health probes are silent. All API reads are audited. No purge.

components.name: Remit ledger tables
components.role: remit_quotes, remit_payments (PK = client-supplied payment_id), remit_events (UNIQUE payment_id+seq), remit_travel_rule, remit_idempotency (PK org_id+idem_key), remit_webhook_deliveries (outbox, no FK, no org_id index), remit_manifests (UNIQUE org_id+date), institutions (registry)
components.tech: Amounts are VARCHAR(64) strings; request_body/verdict/package_json/payload/body are MEDIUMTEXT JSON
components.notes: Indexes remit_payments_org(org_id,created_at), remit_payments_org_state(org_id,state,created_at), remit_payments_anchor(attestation_id), remit_webhook_pending(status,next_attempt_at); FK indexes on remit_payments(quote_id), remit_travel_rule(payment_id), remit_quotes(org_id), institutions(org_id). Nothing runs in a transaction.

components.name: PoR tables
components.role: por_snapshots (signed statement, commitment, totals, challenge, reserves report)
components.tech: Index por_snapshots_org(org_id, created_at); MEDIUMTEXT JSON columns
components.notes: Low write volume (periodic snapshots). Duplicate submissions are blocked by an in-process Map queue, not by a unique key. Public verification is primary-key reads only.

components.name: Background database consumers
components.role: BatchWorker (pendingCount, seal, anchor, confirm, hourly free-tier purge) and RemitWorker (promoteAnchored, deliverDue)
components.tech: setInterval timers in the single Node process; a running flag prevents overlapping ticks
components.notes: BatchWorker runs every 3000 ms live and seals one batch per tick. RemitWorker runs every 2000 ms (hardcoded) and delivers at most 20 webhooks per tick.

components.name: Migration and parity tooling
components.role: One-shot SQLite to MySQL copy; MySQL adapter parity test
components.tech: node:test; parity test runs only when STONEHASH_TEST_MYSQL_URL is set
components.notes: Parity covers bootstrap, rowseq hygiene, rollback, REPLACE, keyset search and LIKE escaping. It does not cover sealBatch/anchor/confirm on MySQL, concurrency, duplicate-key mapping, INSERT IGNORE, the ON DUPLICATE KEY 'AS new' upsert, or dashboard SQL.

capacity_findings.title: Batch worker reads the whole attestations table on every tick (inscription poll)
capacity_findings.claim: refreshConfirmations runs on every worker tick and filters attestations on kind/status/reveal_txid. No index starts with any of those columns, so every tick reads the whole table. Ticks never overlap and seal one batch each, so the scan time sets the tick period and the sealing rate. Throughput falls as the table grows, and organisation rows never expire.
evidence: service.ts:566-567 "SELECT id, reveal_txid, reveal_tx_hex, leaf_bytes FROM attestations " + "WHERE kind = 'inscription' AND status != 'confirmed' AND reveal_txid IS NOT NULL"
db.ts:693-696 attestation indexes lead on batch_id, expires_at or org_id only
worker.ts:68 if (this.running) return; // a slow chain must not overlap ticks
capacity_findings.quantification: The table grows 86.4k / 8.64M / 86.4M rows a day at T1/T2/T3. Sealing rate is about 1024 / max(3 s, scan time): a 30 s scan caps it near 34 leaves/s, below T2's 100/s. At T1 confirmations slow down over months; at T2 the backlog spirals within weeks.
capacity_findings.fix: Poll only status='submitted' rows through an index (kind, status) or a small pending-inscriptions table. Better, keep pending inscriptions out of the attestations scan altogether.
capacity_findings.affects: Attest batching and confirmations; IO for all OLTP traffic

capacity_findings.title: sealBatch writes one row at a time, one batch per tick, selection not served by an index
capacity_findings.claim: Each seal is one transaction of 2N+1 sequential statements. Per leaf it runs an UPDATE by primary key and an INSERT into merkle_proofs. Only one batch of up to 1,024 leaves is sealed per tick. The head and pending selections order by (created_at, rowseq), but rowseq is not in any (batch_id, ...) index, so MySQL sorts all pending rows each time. Rows are not claimed with FOR UPDATE / SKIP LOCKED, and the UPDATE does not check batch_id IS NULL. Two concurrent sealers are stopped only by the merkle_proofs primary key, which makes the second fail with a duplicate-key error.
evidence: service.ts:503-506 for (const [i, r] of pending.entries()) { ... await upd.run(batchId, i, r.id); await ins.run(r.id, batchId, i, JSON.stringify(p.siblings), ...
service.ts:476 WHERE batch_id IS NULL ORDER BY created_at ASC, ${ord} ASC LIMIT 1
db.ts:694 CREATE INDEX attestations_open_order ON attestations(batch_id, created_at)
worker.ts:74-77 // One batch per tick ... const batchId = await this.svc.sealBatch();
capacity_findings.quantification: N=1024 means 2,049 calls per seal (about 0.2-0.5 s on localhost) holding 1 of 10 connections. Maximum sustained sealing is 1024 leaves per 3 s tick, about 341/s. At T3 the backlog grows by at least 659/s, and pendingCount and both selections slow down every tick. merkle_proofs stores about 0.86 KB per leaf (10 siblings x 66 chars) versus 64 B per leaf if the tree were stored once per batch.
capacity_findings.fix: Use a multi-row INSERT for proofs and a single UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...). Add an index (batch_id, org_id, rowseq) or order by rowseq alone. Seal several batches per tick, claiming rows with SKIP LOCKED. Store each batch's tree once and derive proofs at export.
capacity_findings.affects: Attest throughput ceiling and merkle_proofs storage

capacity_findings.title: One 10-connection pool, unbounded wait queue, no acquire timeout, analytics on the same pool
capacity_findings.claim: Every statement for API traffic, console analytics, workers and N+1 fan-outs shares 10 connections. A request that cannot get a connection waits indefinitely: queueLimit is 0 and mysql2 has no acquire timeout. Each statement holds a connection for a round trip plus, for writes, a durable commit, because almost everything autocommits. Dashboard and ledger requests use Promise.all and take 5 to 100 queued slots at once.
evidence: console.ts:694 const [...] = await Promise.all([ (5 lifetime COUNTs)
remit/routes.ts:441 const data = await Promise.all(page.items.map(async (p) => ({ ... await d.svc.get(...)
capacity_findings.quantification: Ceiling is about 10 / (connection-hold time per request). Attest API: 5 statements incl. 2 commits, about 1-5 ms, so roughly 2,000-10,000 req/s at most before other costs. Remit: about 60 commits per payment, so T2 needs about 6,000 commits/s, at or beyond what 10 connections with fsync per commit can do. A dashboard holds 5 connections for as long as its whole-history COUNTs run.
capacity_findings.fix: Make the pool size configurable and larger (30-50, within max_connections). Set queueLimit and request deadlines. Give analytics a separate pool or a replica. Group each request's writes into one transaction.
capacity_findings.affects: Every request's latency under load; worker progress

capacity_findings.title: Synchronous audit INSERT on every audited request, including API reads
capacity_findings.claim: The router waits for the audit_log INSERT to commit before sending the response. Only console screen GETs and health probes are exempt, so every keyed API read becomes a write plus a durable commit. audit_log is keyed on random UUIDs and never purged.
evidence: server.ts:216-218 if (this.onDoneHook) { try { await this.onDoneHook(ctx, reply ? reply.status : res.statusCode, ...
routes.ts:132-133 if (!ctx.audit || !isAudited(method, ctx.path)) return; await recordAudit(d.db, ctx.audit, {...})
capacity_findings.quantification: At least one row per API call: at least 86k/day (T1), 8.6M/day (T2), 86M/day (T3); about 0.45 KB/row with indexes, so at least 14 GB/yr, 1.4 TB/yr and 14 TB/yr. Bank status polling multiplies it.
capacity_findings.fix: Buffer audit rows and write them asynchronously in multi-row INSERTs (or ship them to a log pipeline). Exempt or sample idempotent GETs. Partition by month and archive.
capacity_findings.affects: Latency and commit rate of every API call; storage

capacity_findings.title: Every table except the free tier grows without limit; no purge, partitioning or archive
capacity_findings.claim: Organisation records never expire: issue() refuses an expiry and a boot-time UPDATE clears old expiries. The only purge deletes free-tier attestations hourly. purgeExpiredSessions exists but nothing calls it. Delivered webhooks, idempotency rows, expired quotes, events and audit rows are never deleted, and no table is partitioned.
evidence: service.ts:157-158 if (opts.expiresAt !== undefined && opts.source !== 'public') { throw new Error('only free-tier records expire; ...
account.ts:208-209 export async function purgeExpiredSessions(db: Db) ... DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at <= ? (no caller in src)
capacity_findings.quantification: Attest: about 3 rows and about 3 KB per attestation incl. indexes (attestations about 1.1 KB, merkle_proofs about 1.4 KB, audit about 0.45 KB), so about 0.26 GB/day (95 GB/yr) at T1, 26 GB/day (9.5 TB/yr) at T2, 260 GB/day (95 TB/yr) at T3. Remit: about 33 rows and about 60-90 KB per payment, so about 5-8 GB/day at T1 and 0.5-0.8 TB/day at T2. The box has 572 GB free. Binlog and backups are extra.
capacity_findings.fix: Range-partition append-only tables by month. Archive cold partitions to cheaper storage rather than deleting, since organisation records are kept. Add TTL purges for idempotency (e.g. 7-30 days), delivered webhooks, expired quotes and sessions (wire up purgeExpiredSessions).
capacity_findings.affects: Disk, buffer-pool hit rate, backup/restore time, schema-change time

capacity_findings.title: Random UUID string primary keys and text-encoded binary/time columns, with a stock 128 MB buffer pool
capacity_findings.claim: Hot tables are keyed on randomUUID() stored as VARCHAR(64), so every insert lands on a random clustered-index page. That 36-byte key is repeated in every secondary index. Digests are hex CHAR(64), timestamps VARCHAR(40), ids text. The MySQL config file does not set innodb_buffer_pool_size, so the 128 MB default applies (live value unverified) on a 15 GB box. Once tables outgrow memory, inserts turn into random disk reads.
evidence: db.ts:434 id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,  (with service.ts:171 const id = randomUUID();)
db.ts:437 leaf_bytes CHAR(64) NOT NULL,  db.ts:443 created_at VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
audit.ts:118 randomUUID() as audit_log PK; store.ts:257 randomUUID() as remit_events PK
/etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf sets only bind-address, key_buffer_size, max_binlog_size, log_error
capacity_findings.quantification: attestations carries about 540 B of secondary-index data per row across 6 indexes. Attest data passes 128 MB within the first day at T1 (0.26 GB/day). UNIQUE(org_id, leaf_bytes) also receives random inserts within each org.
capacity_findings.fix: Use ordered keys (UUIDv7, or a BIGINT primary key with the UUID as a unique secondary), BINARY(16) ids, BINARY(32) digests and DATETIME(3). Size the buffer pool to RAM, ideally on a dedicated DB host. Needs a migration plan, because the tables never shrink.
capacity_findings.affects: Insert latency and IO for attestations, merkle_proofs, audit_log, remit_events, webhook rows

capacity_findings.title: Remit uses about 150 statements and about 60 commits per payment; the payment row is rewritten about 13 times; the registry is read in full 4 times
capacity_findings.claim: Each orchestrator step is built from small autocommit helpers. transition does SELECT *, UPDATE, SELECT *; notify does SELECT *, a subscription read and a webhook INSERT; appendEvent does MAX(seq), INSERT, SELECT. registry.list(), a full ordered read of institutions, runs for keyring, snapshot and twice in requireSettlementEntity. The evidence package stores the whole registry snapshot and a copy of every event inside the payment row.
evidence: store.ts:291-293 UPDATE remit_payments SET state = ?, updated_at = ? WHERE id = ? ... return (await this.get(paymentId))!;
orchestrator.ts:130-131 const fresh = (await this.d.store.get(p.id))!; await this.d.outbox.enqueue(p.org_id, await this.webhookUrl(p.org_id), ...
registry.ts:62 SELECT * FROM institutions ORDER BY created_at
capacity_findings.quantification: Commits per second: about 60 at T1, 6,000 at T2, 60,000 at T3. The full payment row (20-40 KB when finished) is read back about 30 times per payment. Institutions read per payment = 4 x the platform-wide institution count, and package_json grows about 0.5-0.7 KB per registered institution.
capacity_findings.fix: Run one transaction per step (event, state change and outbox row together) and avoid the re-reads. Cache the registry in memory with version invalidation. Reference the registry snapshot by hash/version instead of embedding it. Keep large JSON off the hot row.
capacity_findings.affects: Remit throughput, commit rate, storage, binlog volume

capacity_findings.title: Remit/PoR state changes are unguarded read-check-write with no transactions, no compare-and-set and no retry
capacity_findings.claim: Event sequence numbers come from MAX(seq)+1 with no lock. State changes are checked in JavaScript and then written with an UPDATE that does not include the expected old state. Duplicate checks are read-then-insert. Nothing uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, SKIP LOCKED or deadlock retry. A concurrent BFI callback, the async pipeline and the worker can therefore collide: the loser gets a UNIQUE(payment_id, seq) violation, which surfaces as HTTP 500, or a state is lost or moves backwards. SQLite runs one statement at a time, so the tests cannot surface this.
evidence: store.ts:254-256 'SELECT COALESCE(MAX(seq), -1) + 1 AS n FROM remit_events WHERE payment_id = ?' then INSERT (no tx, no lock)
store.ts:291 'UPDATE remit_payments SET state = ?, updated_at = ? WHERE id = ?' (no AND state = ?)
routes.ts:120 return new HttpResult(500, { error: 'internal', message: e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e) });
capacity_findings.quantification: Collisions grow with concurrent writers per payment: rare at T1, routine at T2. Duplicate-key races return 500 with the engine message instead of 409.
capacity_findings.fix: Use db.tx per step with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the payment row (or UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND state=? and check affected rows). Retry on ER_DUP_ENTRY / ER_LOCK_DEADLOCK and map duplicate keys to 409.
capacity_findings.affects: Remit correctness under concurrency; error rates

capacity_findings.title: Webhook outbox: sorts all due rows each tick, delivers at most 20 per 2 s, never purged
capacity_findings.claim: deliverDue filters through the (status, next_attempt_at) index but orders by created_at, which is not in it, so every due row is sorted before LIMIT 20. Deliveries are sequential with a 5 s timeout, and the remit tick is fixed at 2 s. Each payment emits about 11 webhooks. Delivered and exhausted rows are never deleted.
evidence: webhook.ts:78-79 WHERE status = 'pending' AND next_attempt_at <= ? ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20
db.ts:703 CREATE INDEX remit_webhook_pending ON remit_webhook_deliveries(status, next_attempt_at)
main.ts:102 new RemitWorker(orchestrator, outbox, cfg.workerTickMs > 0 ? 2_000 : 0, log)
capacity_findings.quantification: Delivery ceiling is about 10/s. At 1 payment/s (T1), about 11 webhooks/s are queued when banks register a webhook_url, so the pending backlog grows and the per-tick sort grows with it. About 11 rows of about 0.8 KB each are kept per payment.
capacity_findings.fix: ORDER BY next_attempt_at (matches the index) or index (status, next_attempt_at, created_at). Deliver in parallel with SKIP LOCKED claiming. Delete delivered rows after N days.
capacity_findings.affects: Bank notification latency; outbox table growth

capacity_findings.title: Console, billing and dashboard queries count each organisation's whole history on the OLTP pool
capacity_findings.claim: The dashboard counts attestations by status, product, statement and issuer_trust with no index beyond org_id, which means one clustered lookup per historical row. It sums today's payments with substr(created_at,1,10)=?, which cannot use an index. It groups remit_webhook_deliveries by org_id with no org_id index (whole-table scan) and runs a correlated subquery over exhausted deliveries whose cost grows with the square of their number. Quota runs a monthly COUNT twice per console create, and the products page runs 5 monthly COUNTs.
evidence: console.ts:704 SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM attestations WHERE org_id = ? AND status != 'confirmed'
console.ts:709-710 SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM attestations WHERE org_id = ? AND product = 'attest' GROUP BY status
console.ts:778 SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM remit_webhook_deliveries WHERE org_id = ? GROUP BY status
console.ts:861-863 AND d.id = (SELECT d2.id FROM remit_webhook_deliveries d2 WHERE d2.org_id = d.org_id AND d2.payment_id = d.payment_id AND d2.status = 'exhausted' ORDER BY ...
capacity_findings.quantification: At T2 one organisation reaches about 260M attestations in a month and about 3B in a year, so each dashboard view runs 4+ COUNTs over billions of rows on up to 5 pooled connections. Quota cost grows through the month (up to about 260M rows at T2).
capacity_findings.fix: Keep per-org/day/product/status counter or rollup tables, updated in the write transaction. Use created_at ranges instead of substr. Index remit_webhook_deliveries(org_id, status, payment_id, created_at). Move analytics to a replica or separate pool.
capacity_findings.affects: Console responsiveness and pool starvation of API traffic

capacity_findings.title: API request paths with scans or per-row work: free-tier duplicate lookup, ledger search, daily manifest, tx view
capacity_findings.claim: findPublicByDigest omits org_id, so UNIQUE(org_id, leaf_bytes) cannot serve it and it scans the table. Ledger search runs COUNT(*) on every page and, with q, runs 3 EXISTS subqueries with JSON_EXTRACT over every event of every org payment, twice. The daily manifest filters on substr(created_at,1,10), which cannot use an index. The console tx view combines OR with IN (subquery), so it reads every org row.
evidence: service.ts:389 SELECT * FROM attestations WHERE leaf_bytes = ? AND source = 'public'
store.ts:194-195 SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM remit_payments WHERE ${where.join(' AND ')}
remit/routes.ts:588 SELECT id FROM remit_payments WHERE org_id = ? AND substr(created_at, 1, 10) = ? ORDER BY created_at
console.ts:481-482 WHERE org_id = ? AND (reveal_txid = ? OR commit_txid = ? OR batch_id IN (SELECT batch_id FROM anchor_txs WHERE txid = ?))
capacity_findings.quantification: Ledger search with q costs O(org payments x about 14 events) JSON parses, twice per page. The manifest reads the org's entire payment history once per day (index-only). The free-tier scan is bounded by the 500/h global limit.
capacity_findings.fix: Add AND org_id = publicOrgId. Make the total approximate, capped or optional. Copy searchable references (UETR, bank_reference, instruction ids) into indexed columns or a lookup table. Use date ranges. Keep a txid to attestation lookup table.
capacity_findings.affects: Bank-facing ledger and manifest endpoints; free tier

capacity_findings.title: Too many distinct prepared statements: dynamic SQL through execute() can exhaust server-wide max_prepared_stmt_count
capacity_findings.claim: Every statement goes through conn.execute(), which prepares it on the server, and mysql2 caches up to 16,000 per connection. Several queries put LIMIT values, IN-list lengths or filter combinations directly into the SQL text, so each variant becomes a separate statement. The caller controls the IN-list length through state=a,a,a,..., since duplicates are not removed. 10 connections x 16,000 exceeds MySQL's server-wide default of 16,382, which is shared with the other apps on this mysqld.
evidence: audit.ts:211 ORDER BY at DESC, id DESC LIMIT ${limit + 1}
mysql2 lib/base/connection.js:127-131 this._statements = createLRU({ max: this.config.maxPreparedStatements, onEviction: ... statement.close()
capacity_findings.quantification: Audit search alone can produce 64 filter combinations x 200 limits = 12,800 SQL texts. Settlement search variants are unbounded. Once the limit is reached, new prepares fail across the whole server (ER_MAX_PREPARED_STMT_COUNT_REACHED).
capacity_findings.fix: Set maxPreparedStatements to about 256. Use pool.query() for dynamic SQL, or bind LIMIT and de-duplicate and cap the state list.
capacity_findings.affects: Availability of the whole mysqld, including other apps on the box

capacity_findings.title: Several app instances or read replicas would break: workers without claims, in-process dedupe, read-your-writes assumptions
capacity_findings.claim: Both workers would run in every instance with no leader election or row claiming. Concurrent sealBatch runs fail on merkle_proofs duplicate keys, deliverDue sends the same webhooks twice, and promoteAnchored can append duplicate events. PoR duplicate snapshots are prevented by an in-memory Map that assumes one process. Writes are immediately read back (insert then get; the audit screen is expected to show a call right away), so those reads must stay on the primary.
evidence: por/routes.ts:294-299 One process serves this API (see service.ts), so a queue in memory is enough to close that. const queued = new Map<string, Promise<unknown>>();
audit.ts:5-8 written ... before the response goes out, so a reader who asks right after a call already sees the call
webhook.ts:77-80 deliverDue selects due rows with no claim/lock
capacity_findings.quantification: Today: pm2 fork mode with 1 instance. Horizontal scale needs these fixed first.
capacity_findings.fix: Use an advisory lock (GET_LOCK) or a leader lease for the workers, or claim work with SKIP LOCKED plus a claimed_by column. Enforce PoR dedupe with a unique key. Route read-after-write paths to the primary and only lag-tolerant reads to replicas.
capacity_findings.affects: Scale-out of the app tier

capacity_findings.title: Sharding by org_id has exceptions: global client-supplied payment ids, batch tables without an org column, one shared public org
capacity_findings.claim: Almost every query filters by org_id, so org_id is the natural shard key. However, remit_payments is keyed by the bank-supplied payment_id across all tenants, and duplicate checks and partner callbacks look it up by id alone. batches, anchor_txs and merkle_proofs have no org_id. All free-tier records belong to one org, which would be a hot shard. institutions is global reference data.
evidence: db.ts:574 id VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, (remit_payments)
orchestrator.ts:603 const p = await this.d.store.get(paymentId); (BFI callback, no org)
capacity_findings.quantification: Two banks using the same payment_id: the second gets 409 duplicate_payment, which also tells it the id exists for another tenant.
capacity_findings.fix: Key payments on (org_id, payment_id) or an internal id, with a routing table for callbacks. Add org_id to batches. Treat the public tier as its own shard. Replicate orgs, api_keys and institutions as reference data.
capacity_findings.affects: Future partitioning/sharding; tenant isolation of payment ids

capacity_findings.title: Stock MySQL durability and binlog defaults multiply writes of large rows
capacity_findings.claim: No InnoDB or binlog tuning is set in /etc/mysql, so MySQL 8.0 defaults apply: fsync on every commit (flush_log_at_trx_commit=1, sync_binlog=1), binlog on with ROW format and FULL row images. Each UPDATE of a large MEDIUMTEXT row logs both the before and after image in full. The payment row is updated about 13 times, and attestations are updated 3 times each. Live values were not checked because the lead is collecting them.
evidence: /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf: [mysqld] bind-address, mysqlx-bind-address, key_buffer_size = 16M, myisam-recover-options, log_error, max_binlog_size = 100M
store.ts:291 / store.ts:302 UPDATE remit_payments ... WHERE id = ? (about 13 per payment)
capacity_findings.quantification: If FULL images are in use: about 0.5-1 MB of binlog per payment (13 x 2 x 20-40 KB), i.e. about 50-100 MB/s at T2. Attest about 3 KB per attestation, i.e. about 26 GB/day at T2, kept about 30 days by default.
capacity_findings.fix: binlog_row_image=MINIMAL or NOBLOB. Keep blobs off rows that are updated often. Size the redo log and buffer pool. Put the DB on dedicated storage and host; add monitoring.
capacity_findings.affects: Disk IO, disk space, replication lag

capacity_findings.title: Schema changes run inline at boot (synchronous CREATE INDEX before the server listens)
capacity_findings.claim: bootstrapMysql builds any missing index and adds any missing column before the server starts. There is no versioned migration step, so adding an index in a future release blocks startup for as long as the build takes, and several instances would each try it.
evidence: db.ts:975-978 for (const { name, ddl } of MYSQL_INDEXES) { if (existing.has(name)) continue; await pool.query(ddl); }
db.ts:957-966 ADDED_COLUMNS loop runs ALTER TABLE at boot
capacity_findings.quantification: On a table of 100M+ rows (about 12 days at T2), one secondary index build takes tens of minutes to hours of downtime. ADD COLUMN at the end is INSTANT in 8.0, so it is cheap.
capacity_findings.fix: Move schema changes to a separate versioned migration tool and run large DDL online outside the boot path.
capacity_findings.affects: Deploys and restarts

capacity_findings.title: SQLite and MySQL behave differently in ways the SQLite-based tests cannot catch
capacity_findings.claim: Tests run on SQLite, which executes one statement at a time, so MySQL concurrency races (DB-08) never appear. The MySQL parity test is skipped unless STONEHASH_TEST_MYSQL_URL is set and covers few paths. Column limits differ: idem_key VARCHAR(191) while the route only checks a minimum length of 8; content_type VARCHAR(255); label and slug VARCHAR(191); TEXT tops out at 64 KB; INT is 32-bit. The db.ts comment says MEDIUMTEXT NOT NULL columns get expression defaults, but the DDL gives them none. Upsert syntax differs (INSERT IGNORE vs ON CONFLICT; ON DUPLICATE KEY with 'AS new' needs MySQL 8.0.19+). JSON_EXTRACT returns quoted JSON on MySQL. Duplicate-key errors come back as 500 with engine-specific text. One thing does match: mysql2's FOUND_ROWS flag makes affectedRows count matched rows, like SQLite.
evidence: test/mysql-parity.test.ts:22 skip: SERVER === '' ? 'STONEHASH_TEST_MYSQL_URL not set — MySQL parity not exercised' : false
db.ts:631 idem_key VARCHAR(191) NOT NULL,  vs remit/routes.ts:396 if (typeof idemKey !== 'string' || idemKey.length < 8) {
db.ts:396-397 comment 'the three that had one use an expression default' vs db.ts:439 descriptor MEDIUMTEXT NOT NULL, (no DEFAULT)
remit/routes.ts:625-626 VALUES (?, ...) AS new ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
capacity_findings.quantification: Example: an Idempotency-Key longer than 191 characters makes REPLACE fail after the payment was already accepted. MySQL returns 500 and the bank's retry gets 409 duplicate_payment. SQLite accepts it.
capacity_findings.fix: Run the core suite against MySQL in CI, including concurrency tests. Validate input lengths against column sizes. Give MySQL TEXT columns explicit DEFAULT expressions or fix the comment.
capacity_findings.affects: Production-only failures

capacity_findings.title: Inscriptions are swept into digest batches (no kind filter in batching queries)
capacity_findings.claim: inscribe() inserts rows with status 'submitted' and batch_id NULL. pendingCount, the sealBatch head and the pending selections only filter batch_id IS NULL. Inscriptions therefore get sealed into the org's next digest batch, which writes an extra merkle_proofs row and moves their status back from 'submitted' to 'batched'. No test combines an inscription with a seal. This is a correctness issue, not a capacity one.
evidence: service.ts:226-229 INSERT INTO attestations (... status, ... kind, commit_txid, ...) VALUES (..., 'submitted', ..., 'inscription', ...)  (no batch_id)
service.ts:476 WHERE batch_id IS NULL ORDER BY created_at ASC, ${ord} ASC LIMIT 1
grep src: no "kind = 'digest'" or other kind filter anywhere
capacity_findings.quantification: One extra proof row and one status regression per inscription.
capacity_findings.fix: Add kind = 'digest' to pendingCount and both sealBatch selections, with a matching index.
capacity_findings.affects: Status correctness of inscriptions

capacity_findings.title: Hot single-row lookups are index-served
capacity_findings.claim: API key by UNIQUE key_hash, session by primary key, duplicate digest by UNIQUE(org_id, leaf_bytes), payment by primary key, events by UNIQUE(payment_id, seq) (MAX(seq) is answered from the index alone), idempotency by primary key, subscription by UNIQUE(org_id, product), manifest by UNIQUE(org_id, date), and bundle export through four key lookups.
evidence: db.ts:415 key_hash VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
capacity_findings.quantification: Each costs O(log N) regardless of tier.
capacity_findings.affects: Auth, dedupe, payment reads

capacity_findings.title: Keyset pagination with matching indexes; newest-first lists stop at LIMIT
capacity_findings.claim: Audit and settlement lists page on (at, id) and (created_at, id) keyset cursors backed by (org_id, at, id) and (org_id, created_at) with the primary key appended. The attestation list scans (org_id, created_at) newest first with LIMIT at most 500. LIKE wildcards are escaped the same way on both engines.
evidence: db.ts:704 CREATE INDEX audit_log_org_at ON audit_log(org_id, at, id)
service.ts:368 WHERE a.org_id = ? ORDER BY a.created_at DESC LIMIT ?
capacity_findings.quantification: Unfiltered pages cost O(page size). Cost grows only when filters outside the index are selective (see DB-11).
capacity_findings.affects: Console and API lists

capacity_findings.title: No network call inside a database transaction
capacity_findings.claim: Anchor submission, inscription broadcast, reserve measurement and partner calls all happen before or between transactions. Transactions only hold locks for local statements, and the connection is released in finally.
evidence: service.ts:523-526 const handle = await this.backend.submit(payload); ... await this.db.tx(async (tx) => {
service.ts:222 const r = await this.inscriber(body, contentType);  (before INSERT)
capacity_findings.quantification: Lock hold time is bounded by local statement time (the seal transaction is the longest, about 0.2-0.5 s at N=1024).
capacity_findings.affects: Lock contention

capacity_findings.title: Unique keys act as fail-closed backstops
capacity_findings.claim: Even where application checks race, the merkle_proofs primary key (one proof per attestation), UNIQUE(org_id, leaf_bytes), the remit_payments primary key, UNIQUE(payment_id, seq) and UNIQUE(org_id, date) stop duplicate facts from being stored. The losing request errors out instead of corrupting data.
evidence: db.ts:465 attestation_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, (merkle_proofs)
capacity_findings.fix: Map these errors to 409 and retry where appropriate (DB-08).
capacity_findings.affects: Data integrity

scale_path: T2 (about 100/s), in order: (1) Remove the per-tick full scans. Index or restructure the inscription poll (service.ts:564-568, an index on (kind, status)), give anchoredPending (store.ts:307-313) a state-led index or make it event-driven, and make deliverDue order by next_attempt_at. (2) Write batches in bulk. Use multi-row INSERT/UPDATE in sealBatch, an index (batch_id, org_id, rowseq), several batches per tick claimed with SKIP LOCKED, and one stored tree per batch instead of one proof row per leaf. (3) Make each remit step one db.tx with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a state check in the UPDATE, retry on duplicate-key or deadlock, map ER_DUP_ENTRY to 409, cache the registry, and stop re-reading the payment row with SELECT *. (4) Replace whole-history and monthly COUNTs (dashboard, quota, billing, ledger total) with per-org counter tables updated in the write transaction. Make date filters use ranges, add a remit_webhook_deliveries(org_id, status, payment_id, created_at) index, and scope findPublicByDigest by org_id. (5) Pool: make connectionLimit configurable and larger, set queueLimit and request deadlines, cap maxPreparedStatements at about 256 (or use query() for dynamic SQL), and give analytics a separate pool. (6) MySQL: dedicated host or at least a buffer pool sized to RAM, larger redo log, binlog_row_image MINIMAL or NOBLOB, lock-wait and deadlock monitoring. (7) Write audit rows asynchronously in batches, partition audit_log by month, and add TTL purges for idempotency, delivered webhooks, expired quotes and sessions (wire up purgeExpiredSessions). (8) Plan a type migration (ordered keys, BINARY digests and ids, DATETIME(3)); because tables never shrink, it gets costlier the later it starts. T3 (about 1,000/s), additionally: (1) Make the app tier safe to run as several instances: leader lease or GET_LOCK, or SKIP LOCKED claims, for both workers; a unique key instead of the in-process PoR queue; no other process-local assumptions. (2) Add read replicas for reads that tolerate lag (console analytics, ledger search, public verification) and keep read-after-write paths on the primary. (3) Range-partition every append-only table (attestations, merkle_proofs, audit_log, remit_events, webhook deliveries) by time and move cold partitions to an archive tier, since organisation records are never deleted. (4) Shard by org_id: add org_id to batches, anchor_txs and merkle_proofs; key payments on (org_id, payment_id) with a routing table for callbacks; give the public tier its own shard; replicate orgs, api_keys and institutions as reference data. (5) Move large JSON (package_json, request_body, event payloads, webhook bodies) to object storage or compressed columns and keep rows lean. (6) Replace table polling for the audit trail and webhook outbox with a queue or log pipeline.
open_questions: Live MySQL variables are unverified: innodb_buffer_pool_size, innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit, sync_binlog, log_bin/binlog_row_image, max_prepared_stmt_count, transaction_isolation, innodb_autoinc_lock_mode. The config file in /etc/mysql is stock, but SET PERSIST overrides could exist. The lead's live statistics should confirm.

Validate the size estimates against live data: AVG(LENGTH()) of remit_payments.package_json/request_body/verdict, remit_events.payload, remit_webhook_deliveries.body and merkle_proofs.siblings, plus current row counts and data_length/index_length per table. My figures (about 3 KB per attestation, about 60-90 KB per payment) are derived from code shape only.
No EXPLAIN was run (live DB off-limits). Plans for the sealBatch head/pending selections, the console tx lookup, the dashboard COUNTs and the settlement search with q should be confirmed.
Will production run more than one app instance (pm2 cluster or several hosts)? Today it is pm2 fork x1, and the workers, PoR dedupe and rate limiters all assume one process.
Will banks register webhook_url in production? That decides whether about 11 outbox rows per payment are created at all.

For the chain/backend readers: worker.ts:94-95 says a failed anchor 'stays sealed and the next tick retries it', but no query ever selects batches with status 'sealed' (grep), so a failed batch looks orphaned.
For the backend reader: the remit pipeline continues via setImmediate (orchestrator.ts:287-291), with no durable queue or resume sweep after a crash.

Does the owner's never-expire rule cover remit_events, webhook deliveries, idempotency rows, quotes and audit_log, or only attestations? The answer decides whether TTL purges or archive tiers are needed.
Is it intended that all free-tier records share one public org (a single hot partition, and the one shard that must route id-only lookups)?
